commentary.bottom_line: Across mostly offline studies and a few real deployments, recalibrating models or thresholds after drift or updates generally restored calibration or reduced alert burden, though some updates lowered sensitivity or had mixed fairness effects. Certainty is low because outcomes are surrogate measures and few studies compared recalibration triggered by routine monitoring against no recalibration.

perspectives.view: Most studies shown are level 4 offline replays that measure calibration, and one real deployment had a comparator (pmid:40240132). Results mostly favor recalibration, but two studies reported mixed effects (pmid:40079820, epmc:PPR1318939). Outcomes are surrogate measures, and few studies link recalibration to a monitoring trigger, so certainty is low.

A software upgrade raised recall rates about threefold in one screening program (pmid:37293340). Without threshold recalibration, a model update cut specificity to 23.1% with 36.4% more testing (pmid:40233023). Recalibration can also cause harm, since a stale intercept correction reversed bias direction (epmc:PPR1315780) and drift-triggered updating lowered readmission sensitivity below its initial level (pmid:40079820).

In a live deployment, refining alert criteria from reviewed alerts raised median true positive alerts from 47.3% to 78.9% (pmid:38510558). A revised operating point cut alerts from 4.4% to 2.3% with no change in enrolment (pmid:40240132). Weekly retraining on live data maintained model quality elsewhere (pmid:40140275). These reports suggest feedback-driven recalibration can run inside routine workflows.

In one large replay with a racial and ethnic minority focus, effects on fairness gaps varied after drift-triggered updating (pmid:40079820). Another left residual miscalibration in the highest risk percentiles (pmid:41512677). Recalibration of a deployed model improved calibration across race and gender (epmc:PPR749552), and subgroup-targeted updating raised AUPRC by 0.10 (pmid:41726506).

FDA draft lifecycle guidance says manufacturers may plan updates and corrective actions for changing conditions. After an upgrade, the screening program in pmid:37293340 needed thresholds set for each software version. A new model version also shifted specificity until its threshold was reset (pmid:40233023). This suggests sites may need to recheck thresholds after vendor updates.

In one offline cohort, a single logistic recalibration largely corrected prevalence-driven shifts in both directions (epmc:PPR1282655). This suggests simple methods may suffice in many cases. The deployment in pmid:40240132 roughly halved alert volume, which may reduce review workload. No study reported staffing, cost, or the time needed to monitor drift and carry out recalibration.

commentary.research_gap: No study prospectively compared recalibration triggered by drift, alert-disposition, or update-related monitoring against continued use of an unrecalibrated model while measuring patient outcomes. Studies also have not established which trigger thresholds should prompt reassessment, how often corrections go stale, or what staffing and cost recalibration requires.
commentary.underserved_note: No test of the practice reported including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, although some included older adults or racial and ethnic minority groups. Health systems serving these populations cannot assume that recalibration methods or trigger rules perform the same way for their patients, and they may need to check calibration by subgroup locally.
